label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
**Dear Jonno, re: the coolroom (since you won't stop asking)**

Jonno. Mate. You've messaged me four times about this. I've seen the little "???" under my story. Here's the whole thing in one go so I can stop typing it out in the staff toilet on my break. Everyone else who reads this (hi Mum), you're welcome to come along.

**6.40am, Cup Day**

Tuesday the 3rd. Cup Day. The one day of the year Phil books us out like he's running the MCG. 140 covers for lunch, set menu, three course. Big day, but fine. We'd prepped Monday, everything was sitting pretty in the coolroom, I'd had a solid four and a half hours of sleep. Living the dream.

I rock up at 6.40, open the coolroom door, and it's warm. Not "a bit off" warm. *Warm* warm. You know how it normally smacks you in the face when you walk in? Nothing. It felt like walking into a mate's car that's been parked in the sun. Thermometer says 11 degrees.

Compressor had carked it sometime overnight. Just quietly died in the dark like a coward, on the one night of the year it actually mattered.

I'd love to tell you I sprang into action. What I actually did was stand there holding the door for about ten seconds saying "no" out loud to nobody.

**The situation**

So here's where we're at:

- Raff's off for the day, so it's my kitchen. Lucky me.
- Coolroom's cooked.
- 140 people in suits and fascinators turning up in about five hours expecting three courses and a good time.
- I ring Wally from Coldline. Love Wally. Wally cannot come until Wednesday because the part has to come from Sydney. Of course it does. Everything good in this country comes from Melbourne except fridge parts apparently.

Then I ring Phil. You'll appreciate this. I lay it all out for him: compressor's dead, 11 degrees, full book, no Raff. Phil goes, and I quote, "Just make it work mate."

Just make it work mate. Write that on my headstone. That's not a plan Jonno, that's a vibe. That's a man on his way to a marquee.

**Operation Make It Work Mate**

Right. So we had the two undercounters on the line, the bar fridge, and that's it. Which is nowhere near enough, as you'd know, because you once tried to fit a whole case of eggs in the undercounter and broke eleven of them. Don't think I've forgotten.

So I go next door to Marta. Marta, saint that she is, says we can have half her walk-in. Half. Massive. Absolute legend.

Marta does not do favours for free though. Marta wants payment in croissant credit, which means I am now cooking her staff meal for roughly the next three weeks. I've done the maths and I'll be square around the end of the month, provided I don't need anything else from her, which I definitely will.

Then came the move. Me and Benny had to get 30kg of beef shin from our kitchen down the laneway into Marta's. And what did we have? The milk crate trolley. You remember the milk crate trolley. The one with the wobbly wheel you always said was "fine."

It was not fine Jonno.

It was pissing down too, obviously, because Melbourne. So it's me and Benny pushing 30kg of beef shin down the laneway in the rain and halfway there a wheel just comes straight off. Pings off into a puddle. So now it's three wheels and we're half dragging, half carrying this thing, both drenched, both swearing, Benny laughing so hard he had to stop and put his hands on his knees. We got it there though. Beef was fine. My dignity is still in that laneway somewhere next to the wheel.

Meanwhile Kev, our dishy, the hero of this whole story honestly, dug out the old esky (yes, THAT esky, it still smells like the staff Christmas party) and walked down to the servo and bought 14 bags of ice. Fourteen. The servo guy apparently looked at him and goes "big party?" and Kev just said "yeah mate" and walked out. Didn't even explain. I love Kev.

**The damage**

We lost about $1800 of stock, mostly dairy and the duck legs. RIP the duck legs, they deserved better. Everything that was borderline went in the bin because I'm not making 140 people sick on Cup Day and ending up on the news.

Which brings me to the panna cotta.

**The panna cotta incident**

At 12.15 I had to 86 the panna cotta. Dairy was the main casualty and I just didn't have enough left that I trusted. So dessert became, and I'm not proud of this, "affogato with whatever."

Whatever meaning: whatever biscuits we had, a crumble Benny threw together from the pantry, a bit of the poached fruit we'd made for the entrée garnish. Shot of espresso over vanilla ice cream from the bar fridge, chuck the bits on top, send it.

And people LOVED it. More than the panna cotta. I had three separate tables ask what it was called. One bloke sent his compliments to the chef. I've been perfecting that panna cotta for two years Jonno. Two years. And it got beaten by something I made up in a panic with a bag of Scotch Fingers. I'm still not over it.

**Table 9**

Best moment of the day, hands down. Our dining room window looks straight down the laneway, as you know. So the entire time me and Benny were out there dragging the beef in the rain on a three-wheeled trolley, the early tables had a front row seat.

Lady on table 9, mains go out, she looks at the beef and asks the floor staff, dead serious, if the beef was "free range from the laneway."

I nearly lay down on the floor. Bronte (who was on the floor) said she just smiled and said "locally sourced." Give that girl a raise.

**The sweep**

Oh, and to top it off. Phil does the staff sweep every year, you know how it goes. My horse? **Ice Cold Lad.** I'm not making that up. On the day my coolroom died, I drew a horse called Ice Cold Lad. And it came second last.

The universe was taking the absolute piss and I respect it honestly.

**The actual service**

Here's the thing though, and don't tell anyone I got soft about this. It was the best service we've done all year. Maybe ever.

Everyone was locked in. No one was whinging, no one was going missing for smokes, nobody was arguing about who touched who's mise. Benny was on it. Kev was flying through the pit and running ice in between. Floor staff were spinning the whole thing like it was the plan all along. We were running stuff between three fridges, an esky, and a café next door, and the tickets were going out on time. All 140.

Proper "bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite" energy. Which is honestly how every bistro kitchen runs anyway, we just don't usually have to admit it.

Afterwards we sat out the back with a couple of beers, still damp, and nobody really said much. Just that kind of tired where you're grinning for no reason. You know the one. You used to love that bit.

**Which brings me to you**

Now. Jonno. Let's be honest about something.

You would have lost your mind. Absolutely lost it. You'd have opened that coolroom door and just walked straight back out the front and kept walking. And that's the old you. London you? London you would've cried. You've been over there nine months and you're already saying "cheers" when you mean "thanks" and posting photos of a £7 pint like it's normal. London has made you soft. Don't argue with me, I've seen your Instagram. You had a flat white with a leaf on it and you photographed it.

I'm not saying we needed you there. We were fine. We were better than fine, the affogato's going on the menu.

But the milk crate trolley would've been funnier with you on it. And Benny reckons you would've tried to fix the wheel with gaffer tape and made it worse, and he's right.

Wally came Wednesday, by the way. Part from Sydney. Took him forty minutes. Forty minutes, after all that.

Anyway. Coolroom's cold again. Marta's getting her croissants. Ice Cold Lad is presumably eating hay somewhere, a failure.

Come home ya flog.

— Your favourite sous chef
